transcript.content:
Honestly I'd be surprised if the Moon can be seen right now, but give me your honest estimate anyway.

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-01-20 11:57 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-01-20T10:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 59.542 degrees and its azimuth is 151.107 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 47.814 degrees and its azimuth is 124.404 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 2.74 percent illuminated, 19.022 degrees from the Sun, and 385267.8 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest: **No, you will not be able to see it.**

Even though your app correctly shows that the Moon is physically "above the horizon," there are three scientific reasons why it will be invisible to your eyes in these specific conditions:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Contrast)
This is your biggest hurdle. You mentioned the Sun is at an altitude of nearly 60 degrees. At that angle, the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight (Rayleigh scattering), creating a very bright, high-luminance blue sky. 

The Moon, at only 2.74% illumination, is essentially a thin sliver of rock. The "glare" of the daylight sky is orders of magnitude brighter than the reflected light from a tiny crescent. It’s like trying to see a single dim LED light bulb turned on in the middle of a stadium with the floodlights at full power.

### 2. The Proximity to the Sun
The Moon is only 19 degrees away from the Sun. In astronomical terms, that is very close. Because the Moon is so near the Sun in the sky, it is sitting in the brightest part of the solar glare. The "haze" of the atmosphere near the Sun makes it nearly impossible to distinguish any nearby objects unless they are incredibly bright (like Venus or Jupiter, and even then, only in twilight).

### 3. The Phase (2.74% Illumination)
A 2.74% moon is a very "young" crescent. While these are beautiful in a dark, clear night sky, they lack the surface area to reflect enough light to compete with the sun's presence. Even if it were a Full Moon at 11:57 AM, it would be incredibly difficult to see because of the sky brightness; a 2% crescent has almost zero chance.

**The Verdict:**
If you look toward the azimuth of 124° (roughly East-Southeast), you will see a very bright, washed-out sky. You might see a faint "smudge" if you squint intensely, but for all practical purposes, the Moon is "lost" in the daylight. 

**Your intuition was right—it's effectively invisible!**
